title: When in disgrace: structure and situation
short: One long sentence: a 'When' clause of eight lines describing despair, then a turn ('Yet') to the memory of the beloved.
body: The sonnet is a single sentence. Lines 1-8 form an extended subordinate clause beginning 'When', listing the speaker's misery, envy and self-contempt; the main clause arrives only after the turn in line 9 ('Yet'), and its relief is delayed to line 10 ('Haply I think on thee'). The structure enacts the experience: a long, grinding period of depression followed by a sudden lift. 'Disgrace' means being out of favour, not public scandal; one commentary stresses that it describes a failure to gain standing rather than a fall from it. Biographical readings link the poem to Shakespeare's position as an actor or to the closing of the theatres in the plague years of 1592-94, but there is no evidence for a specific occasion.

title: fortune and men's eyes
short: Fortune, the goddess of chance, and public opinion ('men's eyes') have both turned against the speaker.
body: Fortune is the classical and medieval goddess Fortuna, who raises and lowers people on her wheel without regard to merit. Shakespeare elsewhere in the Sonnets blames 'the guilty goddess of my harmful deeds' (Sonnet 111) for his lot as a public entertainer. 'Men's eyes' adds the social dimension: to be in disgrace is to be looked down on. The two together set up the poem's opposition between external valuation (fortune, rank, wealth, others' esteem) and the inward wealth of being loved, which the couplet will set above kings.

title: beweep ... outcast state
short: To weep over, bewail; the speaker laments his condition as one cast out of society.
body: 'Beweep' (Old English bewepan) is a transitive form of 'weep', meaning to lament or weep over something; its be- prefix gives it the solemn, slightly archaic tone of biblical language (compare 'bewail', 'bemoan'). 'Outcast' means rejected or exiled; commentators suspect deliberate exaggeration, since the speaker goes on to envy others' talents and friends rather than describing real banishment. 'State' is the first of three appearances of the word (ll. 2, 10, 14), each with a different weight: here it is his miserable condition.

title: trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries
short: He pesters a heaven that will not listen with useless complaints; the cursing of fate recalls Job.
body: Heaven is 'deaf' because it does not answer, and the cries are 'bootless' (useless). The speaker's cursing of his fate (l. 4) echoes Job 3:1-3, where Job 'cursed his day' and the night of his conception. The image is answered later in the poem: the 'deaf heaven' of line 3 becomes the 'heaven's gate' at which the lark sings in line 12, so that the same heaven which seemed closed is now reached by song. The verb 'trouble' is pointedly domestic and petty, as if the speaker recognises his complaints as an annoyance.

title: bootless
short: Useless, unavailing: from 'boot', profit or remedy (as in 'to boot').
body: 'Bootless' derives from Old English bot, 'help, remedy, compensation', which survives in the phrase 'to boot' (in addition, as a bonus). A bootless cry achieves nothing. The word is common in Shakespeare (e.g. 'bootless prayers', 'bootless errand') and belongs to the same vocabulary of profit and loss as 'rich', 'possess'd', 'wealth' and 'kings' later in the poem: the speaker's spiritual state is consistently described in terms of economic and social fortune.

title: one more rich in hope
short: Someone with better prospects; the start of a catalogue of envied qualities.
body: The speaker wishes himself like someone 'more rich in hope', with better prospects of advancement. Lines 5-7 then pile up the advantages of other men in a list (prospects, looks, friends, skill, range), using the repeated pronouns 'him ... him ... this man's ... that man's' to suggest that he envies a whole series of people, each for a different gift. The catalogue is an instance of the rhetorical figure of accumulation, and its broken rhythm ('Featur'd like him, like him with friends possess'd') mimics restless comparison.

title: Featur'd like him
short: Having handsome features like another man's: the speaker envies others' looks.
body: 'Featured' means formed or shaped in face and body, here 'good-looking' (OED 'featured' adj., sense 1, with a qualifying word). The repetition 'like him, like him' turns a simple wish into a compulsive one, and different men seem to be meant: one has the looks, another the friends. Readers have connected the envy with the speaker's ageing self-image elsewhere in the Sonnets (e.g. Sonnet 62, 'Beated and chopp'd with tann'd antiquity'), though this poem does not specify what he lacks.

anchor: this man's art, and that man's scope
title: art ... scope
short: Another's skill and another's range of opportunity or intellect; some readers hear a poet envying other writers' art.
body: 'Art' means skill or learning; 'scope' means range, whether of mind, opportunity or freedom of action (OED 'scope' n.2). Because the speaker is a poet, some critics take 'art' as literary skill and connect the line to the rival-poet sonnets (78-86), where Shakespeare depicts himself as outclassed; others warn against narrowly biographical reading, since the sentence presents a general mood of envy. The balanced phrasing ('this man's ... that man's') continues the catalogue begun in line 5.

title: With what I most enjoy contented least
short: Even the things he most delights in now satisfy him least; editors debate what 'what I most enjoy' refers to.
body: The line is a chiasmus of opposites (most/least, enjoy/contented): in depression, even his chief pleasures fail. Editors disagree on what these pleasures are. Some take them as his own art, which he despises in comparison with others'; others, noting that 'enjoy' could mean 'possess', take the line to refer to his possessions or advantages in general; a few hear an anticipation of the beloved, whom he 'enjoys' but has forgotten in his gloom until line 10. The ambiguity prepares the turn, in which what restores him is precisely something he already has.

title: Yet: the volta
short: The turn comes at line 9, but the relief is delayed until line 10, after the speaker has almost come to despise himself.
body: The sonnet keeps the traditional turn after the octave, but makes it gradual. 'Yet' introduces line 9, which still continues the misery ('my self almost despising'), and only with 'Haply' in line 10 does the change arrive. Quatrain and sentence structure therefore pull against each other: the third quatrain is split between despair and joy. Vendler and others note how the rhythm lifts at line 11 as the lark rises, so that the poem's sound mirrors its emotional reversal.

title: Haply
short: By chance, perhaps; the word also suggests 'happily', since the chance thought of the beloved brings happiness.
body: 'Haply' means 'by hap', by chance or perhaps (OED 'haply' adv.). The deliverance is unplanned: the speaker happens to think of the beloved, as if by fortune, so that the 'fortune' that disgraced him in line 1 is answered by a lucky chance. Elizabethan spelling and sound make 'haply' close to 'happily', and many readers hear both senses at once. Note too that he thinks of 'thee', the first appearance of the addressee, delayed until the tenth line.

title: the lark at break of day arising
short: The lark rising at dawn and singing at heaven's gate figures the speaker's lifted spirits; the Quarto puts line 11 in parentheses, leaving the syntax open.
body: The skylark sings as it climbs high into the sky at dawn, a traditional emblem of joy and of the soul's ascent. The syntax is ambiguous: what is like the lark? Either 'my state' (l. 10), which rises from sullen earth and sings, or 'I' who think of the beloved. In the 1609 Quarto line 11 is printed within parentheses and there is no comma after 'earth', so 'From sullen earth' can attach either to the lark's rising or to the singing. Shakespeare uses the same image in Cymbeline 2.3, in the song 'Hark, hark, the lark at heaven's gate sings'. The enjambment across lines 11-12 makes the verse itself climb.

title: sullen
short: Dull, gloomy, heavy; the earth is dark before dawn and reflects the speaker's former melancholy.
body: 'Sullen' derives from a word meaning solitary (Old French solain, from Latin solus) and came to mean gloomy, morose, sluggish or dark-coloured (OED 'sullen' adj.). The earth is 'sullen' because it is still dark at daybreak and because it is heavy and unmoving compared with the soaring lark. The word transfers the speaker's mood to the landscape, recalling his earlier solitude ('I all alone', l. 2).

title: hymns at heaven's gate
short: The lark's song reaches the gate of the heaven that was 'deaf' in line 3: prayer is now answered by praise.
body: The 'deaf heaven' troubled by 'bootless cries' in line 3 is now approached by 'hymns', songs of praise. The poem thus moves from complaint to worship, a religious vocabulary that some critics find daring when applied to human love. 'Heaven's gate' was a conventional phrase for the entrance to paradise and also for the dawn sky, the 'gate' through which the sun rises; both apply to the lark's song at break of day.

anchor: sweet love remember'd such wealth brings
title: such wealth
short: The memory of the beloved's love is a wealth that answers the speaker's envy of those 'more rich in hope'.
body: The couplet translates love into the economic terms the poem has used throughout: the man who wanted to be 'more rich' (l. 5) now possesses 'such wealth'. Note that it is love 'remember'd', not present: the beloved is absent, and the remedy is an act of thought. 'Sweet love' may mean the beloved's love for the speaker, the speaker's love for him, or the beloved himself; the phrase leaves this open.

title: state ... kings
short: He would not exchange his condition even with kings; 'state' plays on condition, rank and royal power.
body: 'State' appears three times (ll. 2, 10, 14), at or near the end of its line. It means first a wretched condition, then a mood that rises like the lark, and finally a status he would not trade for a king's. Since 'state' also meant high rank, pomp, and a kingdom (as in 'affairs of state'), the last use plays on royal estate. The final reversal of the opening is complete: the man in disgrace with fortune now scorns the highest fortune of all. Booth and Vendler discuss the repetition as a structural key to the poem.
